title: What High School Debaters Have Really Been Learning About AI
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard argues that competitive school debate is an underappreciated model for AI readiness. Since August, thousands of middle and high school students have debated whether the United States should impose a moratorium on hyperscale data centers, and at national-circuit level they have argued about extinction risk, military competition with China, electricity prices, water, democratic governance and more. He compiled the arguments from a scouting document of more than 2,100 pages, and most of the post is a structured catalogue of 43 Pro and 41 Con contentions, labelled as descriptions of the evidence rather than endorsements. His framing point is that school conversations about AI literacy mostly concern basic concepts and tools, whereas debaters engage with AI's economic, political, ethical, environmental and military implications. He adds that debate also builds collaboration, adaptation and metacognition, and that the knowledge is used rather than memorised. He closes by asking what learning experiences schools should create in an AI world.
points: Debaters across the country spent a topic cycle on hyperscale data centers and AI, covering economics, security, environment and governance, which gives them a breadth of AI understanding that typical AI literacy programmes do not.
Bauschard contrasts this with school AI readiness efforts that concentrate on introducing basic concepts and tools.
The activity develops skills beyond content, including partner collaboration, adapting to unfamiliar challenges and continuous reassessment of one's own arguments.
Knowledge gained through debate is applied to problems and defended under criticism, which he says makes it more durable than exam-driven memorisation.
The catalogue of 43 Pro and 41 Con arguments is an extended resource, and he notes the main strategic clash is whether a national moratorium would reduce harms or merely relocate construction.
quotes: What strikes me most is how this compares with our conversations about AI literacy and AI readiness in schools.

Those technical skills matter. But look at what these debaters are learning about AI’s economic, political, social, ethical, environmental, and military implications. I struggle to think of any educational experience offering a comparable level of sustained engagement with so many dimensions of AI and its implications for society.

Over the years, I’ve had highly competitive debaters tell me they learned more through debate, both about how to think and about the world, than they learned in all their high school classes combined.
They aren’t simply memorizing information for an exam and forgetting it afterward. They’re actively using knowledge to solve problems, defend positions, and respond to criticism.

Public Forum is a two-on-two format, so students continually work with partners, teammates, and coaches. They must evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of their arguments, respond to unfamiliar challenges, adjust their strategies, and communicate complex ideas to different judges.

In the opening constructive speeches, evidence can account for roughly 95% of what students say. That drops substantially in rebuttals, and by the final speeches, students are primarily analyzing, comparing, and weighing competing arguments.

Think about what it means for students to engage with the world at this level over 30-60+ debates on a topic, and what it suggests about the kinds of learning experiences we should be creating in an AI world.

The most important strategic question running through the entire file is whether a moratorium actually reduces the harms Pro identifies, or simply delays construction in the United States while AI development and infrastructure investment continue elsewhere.
